articles.title: Affordability top of mind for voters in final sprint to midterms: ‘I have to pick between medicine or groceries’
articles.summary: Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising pricesFor millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.In Lorain county, Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and...
articles.full_text:
For millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.
In Lorain county, Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and on pace to break the US record for longest public sector strike.
Ohio voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by more than 5%. As the final day of voting nears, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has a slight lead on Republican Senate incumbent Jon Husted in polling, and the economy has been a key factor in the fight.
“They don’t pay a living wage any more. They used to,” Jones said. “Our healthcare coverage has stayed the same, but the cost of it has changed significantly. It used to be $35 a month for a family. In January it’s going to be $600 a month for a family for the same coverage.”
She said as wages have lagged, with starting pay at about $15 an hour, health insurance costs have eaten up any wage gains to the extent that some employees are making less than when they started.
Negotiations for a new union contract broke down with the county, now led by three Republican commissioners, as workers are pushing for a $1 an hour increase to their base pay.
Daniel Petticord, the deputy director of the Lorain county jobs and family services, said in an email “management believes it recognizes the important efforts of our bargaining unit employees while maintaining fiscal responsibility,” and blamed the union for walking away from negotiations.
“We service the clients of Lorain county that are the poorest of the community, and some of the people that work at jobs and family services qualify for those same services,” Jones said. “We’re hoping that with the Ohio governor election, that we get somebody in there who will be in favor of labor and see the fact that people don’t make a living wage in Lorain county any more.”
In Minnesota, Bob Mattila, a special education paraprofessional in Minneapolis and SEIU Local 284 member, is looking for elected officials who will back state legislation that would increase pay for himself and his co-workers to $25 an hour and to lower their costs for health insurance.
“We simply aren’t paid enough to do the vitally important work that we do,” Mattila said. “I even take state health insurance because they decided I don’t make enough money.
“Money, power and respect. Those three things are critical to what we need out of our work and what we deserve from our elected officials,” he added. “Having very labor-friendly people in places of power is going to give workers like me things that we need to live, because we’re at a point where I can’t afford to put $50 of gas every time when I fill up my car when I’m not even making $25 an hour.”
Labor leaders see a real advantage for Democrats now that so much focus is on the economy.
“The labor movement’s been talking about the issues that affect workers and the kitchen table for decades, and we’re now seeing that everybody else got the memo,” said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, which has been pushing to turn out 16 million union family voters this election.
“It’s pervasive. Everywhere I travel, every campaign that you see is talking about what working people are struggling through, and it’s the cost of gas, groceries, rent and healthcare, but it’s also the fact that our pay just can’t keep up with the rising prices.”
In Detroit, Michigan, another key battleground state, 27-year-old Bailee Porter, who has worked at Detroit Diesel and is a member of the United Auto Workers, has been canvassing for candidates such as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the US Senate, citing his support for Medicare for All, which the UAW has also backed.
She said rising prices of basic necessities have made budgeting and cutting back on essentials like groceries a common worry.
“It’s just costly on every aspect. It’s disrupting people’s routines, so it’s ridiculous. Food, gas. I don’t even want to talk about utility bills. It’s just insane,” said Porter. “Things should be affordable. Your basic necessities have to be affordable. There’s just no other way around it. They have to be. Legislation needs to be changed or enforced or written to where it can help the middle class and labor.”
But the financial struggles experienced by many Americans are unlikely to be easily alleviated no matter who wins the midterms. Joe Biden, the US’s most pro-labor president in recent history, also failed to appease voters who were feeling left behind.
Researchers have noted the federal government’s definition of and tracking of poverty doesn’t account for the struggles Americans are facing, as the federal poverty line is outdated from the 1960s and doesn’t account for geographic discrepancies in costs of living.
“The percent of people that are struggling is so much higher than our official statistics are revealing,” said Dr Stephanie Hoopes, an economist and director of United for Alice. “These are often people who are keeping our economy running smoothly and fueling our economic growth, and yet they’re struggling to support their own families.”
- 41.3% of US households, more than 54.5m households, faced financial hardship in 2024, according to a 2026 report by United for Alice.
- 12.5% of US households made under the federal poverty level threshold, an income of $15,060 annually for a single individual and $31,200 for a family of four.
- 28.8% of US households were Alice: asset limited, income constrained and employed. These households earn above the federal poverty level but did not make enough money to afford basic expenses in the county where they live.
- 2025 and 2026 projected data shows the costs of basic necessities continuing to outpace overall inflation.
“By some measures, our economy is doing great, unemployment rate is low, stock markets booming, productivity and GDP are growing,” Hoopes added. “But when you look at things like how many households are Alice [asset limited, income constrained and employed], and that number continuing to increase, and wages lagging behind the cost of living, there’s some real concerns in the economy.”
For Shunda Whitfield, a certified nursing assistant in St Louis, Missouri, those economic concerns can be life-threatening.
She has been struggling with a recent spike in costs for her medication for lupus, an autoimmune disease.
“I sometimes have to choose between if I’m going to get my medication or if I’m going to get groceries in house due to the fact that my medicine is going up,” said Whitfield, who has been struggling to afford a recent spike in costs for her lupus medication.
“You have to juggle things around to make sure you have cash to get to work to make the money to afford groceries or your medication,” she added. “I would like to see people get out here and vote to put people in place that are for the working people and not just for the billionaires.”

articles.title: The Trump administration wants to give married parents money to stay at home. Will it be enough?
articles.summary: Experts say the proposed program prioritizes parents in ‘traditional families’, ignoring the flexibility needed that all families need to support themselvesErica Hall and her husband knew that raising kids wouldn’t be cheap.They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. articles.full_text:
Erica Hall and her husband knew that raising kids wouldn’t be cheap.
They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. When her first child was born, Hall had to self-fund her maternity leave by drawing on savings. And recently, Hall was laid off from her tech job, leaving her at a crossroads.
“Do we move to a lower-cost daycare? What kind of job should I look for? Can I dial back now?” said Hall, who lives in Seattle. And perhaps the most essential of all questions: “Do we need to completely 100% replace my income?”
More American families than ever consist of two working parents: 52% are dual-income households, compared to 31% in 1975, according to the Pew Research Center. Eight out of 10 of these families say the arrangement has been beneficial to their finances.
Despite this shift in family dynamics, the Trump administration has remained focused on an agenda that emphasizes a “traditional” family structure, where one parent stays home to take care of children.
As part of this agenda, the White House is considering a program that would pay parents $9,000 annually to stay at home, using reallocated funds that are now used for federal programs that typically support single mothers and low-income families, according to the New York Times.
The plan was reportedly proffered by JD Vance, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who has proclaimed himself a defender of “pro-family” policies. The vice-president penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed in 2021 criticizing federal spending on daycare, claiming that “young children from average, healthy homes can be harmed by spending long hours in childcare.”
“It turns out that normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force,” he wrote on social media at the time.
As vice-president, Vance has continued to angle himself as a defender of families. “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families across our country, we have a simple message for them: stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance said at the Republican’s midterm convention in September.
But experts and parents who spoke to the Guardian said the proposed program for stay-at-home parents prioritizes a single type of family structure and ignores the flexibility that families need to support themselves and their children.
“Families of all compositions need help right now. All families do. We should not pit families against each other,” said Chandra Childers, a senior policy and economic analyst at the Economic Policy Institute.
For Natalia Goodnow of Pittsburgh, being a stay-at-home mother of two was a temporary choice that allowed her family to save on the cost of childcare while she went back to school and pursued a second master’s degree. After she graduated, she was forced to delay her next job search after graduating because the waitlist for her child’s daycare, like many in the country, had grew significantly after the pandemic.
Now, Goodnow is balancing taking care of her children while also building up her own consulting business, which she believes will afford her flexibility to work around her daughter’s schedule. She doesn’t expect she’ll ever stop working in some capacity.
“I’m not built to be just a stay-at-home parent,” she said,
There’s also a risk to relying on one parent’s income. Even though her family is able to live “somewhat stable” on just her husband’s income, Goodnow said she’s worried that his career as a physician, combined with the responsibility to support the whole family himself, will lead to burnout.
“I have to have a second income stream created to give him flexibility to scale down, because it’s just not sustainable,” she said, pointing out that the proposed $9,000 wouldn’t be enough to match what she would make if she worked.
Jillian Whitlow, a mom of three who is pregnant with her fourth child, wishes at times that she could stay at home to take care of her children, but after launching a successful marketing business, her husband left his job as a mechanic to take care of their kids.
The choice stemmed from practicality. The cost of daycare for her children was greater than their monthly mortgage payment.
Though Whitlow’s family, who live in Texas, is in a better financial place than they’ve ever been, they still feel the pain of rising costs and are still paying off student debt and loans on their mobile home. Still, Whitlow sees the White House’s proposal as an unnecessary interference in personal family decisions.
“I would love it if there was a lot less government in all of our lives,” she said, “I would love it if each individual family had more freedom to make the decisions that they want to make about the best way to raise their families.”
“It should be up to me and my family to make that decision, and not the government pushing me to stay at home,” Goodnow said.
Childcare costs can pose a major financial burden on families. Forty per cent of households, including those that have one parent who works less than full-time, spend an outsized percentage of their income on childcare, according to a recent report from the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality.
The White House’s plan, by reallocating federal funds from the Department of Health and Human Services that have typically gone to low-income, single-parent families, could actually making childcare even more expensive or less available, Childers said.
“The minute you start draining resources that go into funding this childcare pool, then rates have to rise on other families, some of whom may already be stretching to make it as it is,” she said.
Recent policy changes by the Trump administration may also indirectly make it harder on American families, said Liz Hipple, a policy expert at the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality. Recent pushes to increase the work requirements for Medicaid and Snap benefits, for example, will probably make it harder for some families to support themselves.
Policies that support higher wages or paid parental leave would go much further to support families, she added.
“If the Trump administration was serious about supporting traditional families with one breadwinner, there are plenty of labor policies that they could support,” Hipple said. “Those aren’t the policies that they’re pursuing.”
